title: Ancient Civilizations
theme: Social studies: how early societies rose, ruled and fell
objectives: I can explain what a civilization is and how a food surplus helped early societies grow.
I can use ten history words to describe how societies gained land, held power, and lost it.
I can tell apart words for land and people (territory, inhabit, nomadic) and words for power (empire, dynasty, conquer).
I can write a short explanation of why one society prospered or declined.
rationale: Sixth-grade social studies opens with early states, so three exact terms (civilization, empire, dynasty) are taught beside the verbs and nouns historians use to explain growth and collapse (surplus, conquer, prosper, decline) and the words for land and people (territory, inhabit, nomadic). The order follows the story history textbooks tell: people move, farming creates a surplus, cities and rulers appear, lands are conquered, and power eventually declines. Students need this vocabulary to read, write, and speak about any ancient society in the year ahead.

words.def: A large society with cities, a government, record keeping, and workers who do different jobs.
words.ex: The civilization along the Nile built cities, kept written records, and ran a government that collected taxes.
words.ex2: Pyramids, temples, and written records show that a complex civilization once lived beside the river.

passage.title: How Early Societies Rose and Fell
paras: For most of human history, people lived in small nomadic groups that moved from place to place to follow food and water. They gathered plants, hunted animals, and carried everything they owned. Then, roughly ten thousand years ago, people in several parts of the world began to farm, and daily life slowly changed.

Farming made something new possible: a surplus. A family that grew more grain than it could eat could store the extra or trade it. Because a surplus meant that not everyone had to farm, some people became potters, builders, priests, or record keepers. Villages grew into towns, and towns grew into cities.

Historians use the word civilization for a society that has cities, a government, a way of keeping records, and workers with different jobs. Many early civilizations rose beside rivers. In Egypt, people chose to inhabit the narrow strip of land along the Nile, because the river's yearly floods left behind rich soil that helped farms prosper.

Strong rulers often wanted more land. When an army conquered neighboring peoples, the ruler gained their territory, and a kingdom could grow into an empire, a large realm of many lands and peoples under one government. At its height, the Roman Empire held territory all around the Mediterranean Sea. Power was often passed down within one family, and a line of rulers from the same family is called a dynasty. In China, the Han dynasty lasted for more than four hundred years.

No civilization stayed on top forever. Cities that prospered could decline if crops failed, if rulers fought each other, or if invaders arrived. Because the written records of many ancient societies are incomplete, historians also study the traces they left behind: ruins, tools, coins, and pottery. A persistent researcher can use such clues to build a case about why a great city faded, though the full story may become evident only after years of careful work.

an army that protects a city
a line of rulers from the same family

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for how early societies formed, ruled land, and lost power, read an informational passage about farming, surplus, and civilization, and practice using the words to explain cause and effect in history.

notes.va.civilization.n: Civilization is a label historians use for a type of society, not a ranking of better and worse. Many peoples without cities had rich cultures. Have students list the features in the definition and check an example against them.
notes.va.empire.n: Contrast empire with kingdom: an empire rules many peoples, often by conquest. Students may think an empire needs an emperor; some did not use that title. Use a map to show an empire's size compared with the land of its original city.
notes.va.dynasty.n: A dynasty is about family succession, not about how long a ruler reigned. Draw a simple family tree of rulers on the board. The word names the family and the period of its rule.
notes.va.territory.n: Territory applies to rulers and to animals; the shared idea is control of an area. Use a map to trace a territory's borders. Students may mix territory with terrain; terrain is the shape of the land.
notes.va.conquer.v: Conquer has a historical sense (taking land by force) and a figurative sense (overcoming a fear). Keep the figurative sense short; the historical sense is the focus. Discuss how history is often written from the conquerors' point of view.
notes.va.surplus.n: The key idea in this unit: a surplus lets some people do other jobs. Make a flow chart: surplus, trade, new jobs, cities. Surplus is not the same as waste; it is what remains after needs are met.
notes.va.nomadic.adj: Be careful with stereotypes: nomadic does not mean simple or lost, and some nomadic peoples built large, powerful states. Nomadic describes a way of living, not a level of skill. Contrast with settled farming communities.
notes.va.inhabit.v: Inhabit is a formal word for 'live in' and takes a direct object (inhabit the valley, not inhabit in the valley). Students often add 'in'. Have them rewrite casual sentences with inhabit.
notes.va.prosper.v: Prosper pairs naturally with decline as opposites. It is more than getting rich: it means doing well over time. Ask students what a society needs to prosper beyond money.
notes.va.decline.v: Decline has a size sense (becoming less) and a manners sense (declining an invitation). The unit focuses on the first. Decline is usually gradual; use collapse for something sudden.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says a family that grew more grain than it could eat could store or trade the extra. The extra grain is the surplus. Then it says not everyone had to farm. So surplus is the cause and new jobs are the effect. I will use because to connect them.'

teacher.reviewAdvice: Use trace, evident, and persistent from earlier units when students discuss how historians work: traces left behind, what becomes evident, how persistent research helps. Revisit conquer and decline again in unit 5 when change is the topic.

frames: The society was able to prosper because it had a surplus of ___.
The ruler conquered ___, so the kingdom became an empire.
wida.oral: Partner A tells the story of a society in three sentences using surplus, prosper, and decline. Partner B retells it using the words empire or territory.

needsReview: Fact claims in the passage and word records, believed true but worth a history review: farming began roughly ten thousand years ago in several parts of the world; the Han dynasty lasted more than four hundred years; the Roman Empire at its height held territory around the Mediterranean Sea; the Nile's yearly floods left rich soil; wolves mark territory with scent; cats mark territory by rubbing; several kinds of penguins live on Antarctic coasts.
The features of a civilization (cities, government, record keeping, specialized workers) follow a common textbook list; historians define the term in slightly different ways.
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: excedente, disminuir (decline, 'decaer' also possible), nómada, civilización, imperio.
Sense boundary: conquer and decline each teach one extra sense; confirm they are helpful and not distracting.
Sensitivity: nomadic peoples are described neutrally; a reviewer should confirm the passage does not imply that nomadic cultures were less advanced.
